rationale:
This slate follows the 11-17 growth playbook. Its rule is broad searched long-form only, and its top priority is getting the long video to ship.

**Long video (L1).** It's #1 in the playbook queue: a re-render of the fact-checked 11-14 "Nausea: Foods That May Help" script. That render was held for beat drift and never published, so this isn't a repeat. It's a broad Lane A felt-symptom question, built on label and advisory evidence that's already been verified, and it doesn't need any new research. On the search-demand count, at least 2 of the last 7 long videos already used that format (First Month 11-13, Mounjaro vs Zepbound and Months 2–6 on 11-16), so today's Lane A long video is allowed. If L1 is held again, ship the next ready item in the queue instead.

**Shorts.** All 3 are felt symptoms or practical moments, with tirzepatide first in every title.
- **S1 (08:00):** a new pen "Is this normal?" moment: what the medicine in the window should look like, from the IFU. Pen Shorts are proven winners, and this angle hasn't been used.
- **S2 (13:00):** a spin-off of L1 and the day's myth-check: "Is ginger ale the answer for nausea?"
- **S3 (20:00):** starts the holiday-table run a day early with a rising, low-competition search, travelling with the pen. The angle is flying (carry-on vs checked), which is different from the 11-15 fridge-storage Short.

**Carousel (C1).** The playbook says carousels reuse verified Short text only, so C1 reuses the verified 11-16 dizziness Short.

**What I skipped.**
- **NAION, T-REx, hair, injection site and Keeping Results:** all covered within the last 30 days.
- **News items (teens, the Foundayo pill in Australia):** news Shorts get about 25 views, and the playbook bans approval-status topics.
- **Cost topics:** banned.
- **Caution items (skin dysesthesia, disordered eating):** too likely to be held.

**Body-system spread.** Two pieces are GI (L1, S2). The others are the pen (S1, S3) and circulation/fluids (C1).

**Pillars.** No pillar is used more than twice: get-the-most ×2, life-on-glp1 ×2, myths ×1.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) and food: eating habits and food choices that may ease the common stomach side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, heartburn and burping), why meal size, fat and pace matter when the stomach empties more slowly, and when symptoms mean calling a prescriber
pieces.angle: RE-RENDER ONLY of the verified 11-14 L1 script (playbook queue #1), with no script changes. Rebuild every cut from the final word timestamps. The ship-blockers are measured on the render: every cut within 0.5 s of its beat, masking 0.02 or lower, transcript matching the script word for word, and a description that ends '…whether it's right for you.' Keep the verified content locked. Sentence 1 names tirzepatide and the question, with the short answer by 15 s: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full, easier on greasy food. Second payoff at 15–30 s: the label's pooled nausea rates per dose vs placebo, plus 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'. The advisory's 'first few days' fatty/high-fibre line stays at its exact scope. NHS reflux and dehydration lines are tagged NHS. Include the kidney caveat on protein and the insulin/sulfonylurea low-blood-sugar caveat. Emergency card, then the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Publisher: put a ▶ Watch next link to Side Effects after the first paragraph, and add the video to 'Life on Tirzepatide'. Thumbnail: 'Which Foods Help?'. If the render is held again, ship the next ready queued long video the same day.

pieces.topic: Looking at the medicine in your tirzepatide pen before the shot: what the Instructions for Use say it should look like (colour, clarity, particles), and what to do if it doesn't
pieces.angle: Name the source: 'Zepbound single-dose pen IFU (US)'. If the Mounjaro pen IFU says the same thing at its own working URL, add it as 'Mounjaro pen: same check, see its own IFU'. By 6 s, paraphrase or quote the label: the medicine should be clear and colourless to slightly yellow, and don't use it if you see particles or discolouration. Add 'cloudy' and 'frozen' only if the IFU URL loads and prints them. Scope card: 'US single-dose pen. KwikPens and vials have their own leaflets; check the one in your box.' Untagged line: 'Not sure? Don't use it. Ask your pharmacist or call the number in your IFU.' Drop the injection-site stat card. Keep the closing as planned, with no subscribe or link line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Pen: What Should the Medicine Look Like? #shorts
pieces.why: Visible pen 'Is this normal?' Shorts are our proven 08:00 winners (pen blood 111, injection site 254 and 202). This moment hasn't been covered yet, and the evidence is low-risk and IFU-only. | fact-check: Low risk and useful. I checked the Zepbound label on uspl.lilly.com, which says the medicine is 'clear and colorless to slightly yellow' and 'Do not use ZEPBOUND if particulate matter or discoloration is seen.' 'Cloudy' and 'frozen' are allowed only if the pen IFU's own URL loads and prints them. Air bubbles go in only if that IFU mentions them. 'Tirzepatide pen' is ambiguous: Mounjaro and Zepbound have separate US single-dose pen IFUs, so the Short must name which IFU it is quoting. The optional injection-site stat card (6–8% vs about 2%) has nothing to do with what the medicine looks like, and a viewer could read it as cloudy medicine causing reactions. Drop it.

pieces.topic: Nauseous on tirzepatide: is fizzy ginger ale the answer? What to sip instead, per NHS nausea advice
pieces.angle: Spin-off of L1, asking one fresh question (drinks, not food). 13:00 practical moment and gentle myth-check. Sentence 1 (14 words or fewer): 'Tirzepatide nausea: is fizzy ginger ale really the fix?' By 6 s: NHS nausea advice lists sipping cold drinks and ginger or peppermint tea. Copy the NHS page wording with its live review date, and tag only what it prints. Label fact, separate sentence: tirzepatide delays gastric emptying, and nausea is common, 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time', with one pooled rate per dose vs placebo matching L1's verified script. Untagged: some people find fizzy drinks add to burping, so go easier on them. Sip little and often, unless you've been told to limit fluids. Use the label's dehydration line if you can't keep fluids down. Emergency card: severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, means stop and call your healthcare provider right away. Then the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.', and a loop to sentence 1. Post note: the related-video target is L1 once it's verified live, otherwise Side Effects.

pieces.topic: Flying with your tirzepatide pen for Thanksgiving: carry-on vs checked bag, keeping it in its original labelled box, and storage limits as the label states them
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Flying with your tirzepatide pen? Here's what the label says about storage.' By 6 s, tagged to the Zepbound PI (28 Aug 2026) and the pen IFU's own URL: don't freeze, keep it in the original carton to protect it from light, and the unrefrigerated time and temperature limit exactly as printed. TSA line only as tsa.gov prints it, with its live date (medicines allowed in carry-on; tell the officer about liquid medicines). Untagged tip: 'Many people keep it in their carry-on so they can control how it's stored, in its original labelled box.' Untagged: 'Unsure if a pen is still OK? Ask your pharmacist.' Scope card: US pens; UK/AU packs and KwikPens may differ. No missed-dose or skip-a-dose talk, no dates in narration.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Pen on a Plane: Carry-On or Checked? #shorts
pieces.why: The radar shows travelling with the pen as rising with low competition ahead of Thanksgiving travel week. It starts the holiday series on the curve, and it's about flying, not the 11-15 fridge-storage question. | fact-check: The topic is safe and timely. Tighten sentence 1, though: 'Carry-on or checked bag matters' reads like a sourced claim, but neither the label nor TSA says checked bags damage pens. The safe facts are: the label says don't freeze and protect from light, the label gives an unrefrigerated limit (check the time and temperature at the live PI/IFU URL, with no rounding), and TSA allows medicines in carry-ons. Carrying the pen yourself is our own tip, so it must be untagged and framed as 'so you can control how it's stored'. Thanksgiving belongs only in the post copy and the series log, never as a date in narration. Keep the scope card for US vs UK/AU packs and KwikPens.

pieces.topic: Feeling dizzy or light-headed on tirzepatide: label rates vs placebo, everyday contributors, and when to get help (reused from the verified 11-16 Short)
pieces.angle: Same 7 slides with one fix. Slide 5: 'Label: dehydration can affect the kidneys. Low blood sugar is a higher risk for people with diabetes taking insulin or a sulfonylurea.' Slide 3 ends with: 'Never change blood pressure medicines on your own. Talk to your prescriber.' Slide 6 keeps the emergency number first ('Fainting, chest pain or confusion? Call your local emergency number right away.'), then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Slide 7: 'Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' Drop the carousel if the 11-16 script isn't confirmed verified.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Dizziness: What the Label Shows
pieces.why: The playbook allows carousels only as reused verified Short text. The dizziness Short (11-16) passed QA, so this costs no new research or risk. | fact-check: Reusing the verified text is fine only if the 11-16 dizziness Short is confirmed verified. QA logged a scope slip in that Short: its narration said the higher low-blood-sugar risk applied to everyone. Slide 5's wording as proposed ('a higher risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea') also leaves out the population, so copying it word for word would repeat a known error. Slide 5 must say the risk is higher for people with diabetes taking insulin or a sulfonylurea. Slide 2's population wording matches the pooled-data rule (Study 1 excluded type 2 diabetes; Study 2 enrolled only people with it). All numbers (4/5/4 vs 2, 1/1/2 vs 0, 2.2% vs 1.2%) must match the verified Short and the PI (28 Aug 2026) exactly, each labelled by dose arm. Slide 3 needs the don't-change line spelled out: 'Never change blood pressure medicines on your own; talk to your prescriber.' Untagged tips stay hedged. 'Minimum effort' must not mean templated: the slide designs still need to be original.
